title: Asia stocks slide as AI jitters hit Korean chipmakers
full_text:
Nasdaq surges 1% as tech lifted by SpaceX, Tesla on Musk’s hint at possible merger
Investing.com -- Asian stocks fell on Thursday as mixed earnings from major U.S. technology companies failed to reassure investors about the returns on massive artificial intelligence investments, renewing pressure on semiconductor shares and Chinese equities.
Wall Street closed higher overnight. In Asian trade, Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.2%, while S&P 500 futures dropped 0.6%, after Tesla shares declined 3.3% in after-hours trade following a cut to its capital-spending forecast.
Meta Platforms rose 2.2% after raising its AI spending outlook, while semiconductor equipment maker Lam Research fell 7.4% after issuing a weaker-than-expected earnings forecast.
Brent crude climbed 1.5% to above $110 a barrel after deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened supply concerns, while risks to shipping around the Strait of Hormuz persisted despite a recent acceleration in exports through the waterway.
Korean chipmakers lead Asia selloff as Chinese stocks near bear market
The MSCI Asia Pacific index fell around 1%, with South Korea’s KOSPI declining 2.1% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 losing 1.1%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 2.7%, while China’s CSI 300 slid 1.6% and the Shanghai Composite fell 1.2%.
South Korean chipmakers bore the brunt of the technology selloff, with SK Hynix plunging 4% and Samsung Electronics falling 3.6%. Japan’s Kioxia dropped 3.3% and Murata Manufacturing declined 2.1%. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing slipped 0.6%, while Foxconn fell 1%.
The renewed weakness comes as investors question whether heavy spending on data centres and computing capacity can deliver sufficient returns, with financing costs and stretched valuations adding to concerns about a potential AI bubble.
The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5% last week, its steepest weekly decline since April 2025. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index also suffered an eight-session losing streak, its longest since October 2008.
Separately, South Korea’s central bank left borrowing costs unchanged after two successive rate increases, as policymakers weigh inflationary pressures stemming from the semiconductor-driven economic upswing.
China shares approach bear market as Alibaba leads e-commerce losses
Mainland Chinese equities continued to weaken amid fading hopes for substantial stimulus, lacklustre corporate earnings and lingering anxiety over the global AI trade.
The CSI 300 fell as much as 1.6%, taking its losses from a June peak to around 20% and putting the index on the brink of a technical bear market.
Alibaba led losses among Chinese e-commerce companies after the government called for stronger quality control, with its shares falling 5.5%. JD.com lost 4.2%, Meituan declined 3.9% and Tencent dropped 3%. MiniMax lost 6.8% and Z.AI dropped 8.9%. ChangXin Memory Technologies declined 4.1%.
The market weakness contrasts with the continued willingness of some investors to back individual AI infrastructure companies. South Korean neocloud provider Elice Group rose for a second consecutive session, climbing as much as 25% to 99,900 won in Seoul and moving above its 90,500-won IPO price for the first time since listing.
Elice shares had closed 30% higher on Wednesday, reaching the daily price limit, after plunging around 32% during Tuesday’s debut.
Elsewhere in the region, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.3%, while New Zealand’s NZX 50 dropped 0.4% and Singapore’s Straits Times Index declined 0.2%. India’s Nifty 50 futures slipped 0.3%.
Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite rose 1.1%, recovering some ground after plunging more than 11% last Friday in its steepest one-day decline since January 1998, before extending losses earlier this week. The selloff followed MSCI’s proposal to reclassify Indonesia from emerging-market to standalone-market status.

title: Bank of Korea holds rates at 3% after back-to-back hikes
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Bank of Korea kept its benchmark interest rate at 3.00% on Thursday, giving policymakers time to assess the effects of two consecutive rate hikes on domestic inflation as strong demand for semiconductors continues to underpin economic growth.
The central bank left its seven-day repurchase rate unchanged, as expected by economists. The decision came after two 25-basis-point rate increases in July and August, the central bank’s first back-to-back tightening moves in over three years.
Policymakers opted to take time to evaluate how the earlier increases were affecting domestic demand and price pressures before deciding on further tightening.
The South Korean won strengthened following the decision. The USD/KRW pair fell 0.2% to 1,324.44, indicating a firmer won against the U.S. dollar. South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI index was down 0.7%.
Governor Shin Hyun Song had signalled a gradual approach following the August hike, although the central bank has pledged to maintain restrictive monetary policy until it is confident inflation is converging toward its 2% target.
The decision follows the August rate increase, which drew one dissenting vote in favour of holding rates steady. The central bank’s six-month interest-rate projection also showed a median rate of 3.25%, implying another 25-basis-point increase in the current tightening cycle.
Attention now turns to Shin’s press conference later in the day for further clues on whether policymakers will resume tightening at their November meeting. The governor is expected to explain the board’s reasoning and offer guidance on the policy outlook.
The central bank’s pause comes as South Korea’s semiconductor industry continues to underpin economic growth, supporting exports and domestic activity while adding to demand-side inflation pressures.

title: Fortescue shares hit 16-month low as Q1 iron ore shipments miss estimates

title: Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack, Microsoft says
full_text:
Nasdaq surges 1% as tech lifted by SpaceX, Tesla on Musk’s hint at possible merger
Oct 21 (Reuters) - A Chinese state-aligned hacking group used an AI-driven penetration testing tool to compromise IT services firm ConnectWise as part of a campaign that targeted hundreds of organizations globally, Microsoft said on Wednesday.
Based on Microsoft’s analysis and evidence available to ConnectWise, "it appears that a China state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on ConnectWise Cloud Backup," ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said in a separate statement.
Rivelo said ConnectWise "contained the affected application connections and are restoring services in controlled phases," and that "those actions do not remove unauthorized access that may have already been established within individual customer tenants, which require separate review."
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said China "opposes and fights hacking activities in accordance with the law. At the same time, we oppose smears and attacks against China under the excuse of cybersecurity issues."
The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, used an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign, Microsoft said.
There are multiple tools used to conduct penetration testing, a form of legitimate testing of the security of networks or services. ARTEX allows users to use any AI model to automate a variety of penetration testing tasks and can be configured to run autonomous tasks including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, Microsoft said.
The attack targeted organizations across a variety of sectors, including aerospace, defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, think tanks and non-profit organizations, Microsoft said.
While the majority of targeting was not successful, Microsoft said, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence — or high-level access that could continue even after cleanup efforts — at many organizations in a brief time.

title: Netflix shares fall over 4% on soft current-quarter revenue guidance
full_text:
Nasdaq surges 1% as tech lifted by SpaceX, Tesla on Musk’s hint at possible merger
Investing.com -- Netflix issued current-quarter revenue guidance that missed consensus estimates, sending shares of the company down more than 4% in early U.S. trading.
The streaming giant has been struggling with user engagement and continued capital spending to sustain its vast portfolio of content. Shares of Netflix have fallen 0.4% since the company’s last quarterly report in July, and have lost more than 26% year-to-date, lagging behind a 12.7% rise in the benchmark S&P 500.
Netflix has also seen two high-profile executive departures in the span of a week, with Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria being replaced by former Fox and Disney media executive Peter Rice, and film division head Dan Lin leaving after nearly three years at the helm.
Last week, Netflix said it would eliminate about 1,000 jobs, or 6% of its global workforce, in its biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
To keep viewership elevated, Netflix has been broadening its programming mix beyond on-demand films and television, adding live events, sports, video podcasts and content from YouTube creators. It has also pursued bundling arrangements with other streaming services and secured the rights to broadcast the 2030 FIFA World Cup, in a bid to prop up the amount of time users spend on the platform.
In July, Netflix said it would reduce the frequency of its viewing-hours report, publishing the data annually instead of twice a year starting in January 2027. The firm stopped reporting quarterly subscriber numbers in 2025.
Goldman Sachs recently said third-party data on Netflix’s engagement metrics had been “quite mixed” this summer into fall. Citing Sensor Tower data, the brokerage had highlighted a 10% year-on-year decline in U.S. monthly active users in the third quarter, compared to a 1% decline in the rest of the world.
"We’ll continue to expand our entertainment offering through licensing and new ways to bring in more third-party content to our service, like our TF1 partnership in France. Our audience, which is approaching one billion people, and our best-in-class product capabilities, make us great partners for studios, networks and creative talent," Netflix said in a letter to shareholders.
The streaming firm earned $0.87 per share on revenue of $12.87 billion in the third quarter. Analysts had expected a profit of $0.82 per share and revenue of $12.87 billion.
For the fourth quarter, Netflix projected revenue of $13.4 billion, compared to Wall Street estimates of $13.51 billion. Netflix guided for annual revenue of $51.1 billion, versus $51 billion to $51.4 billion previously.
"While subscription revenue growth has outperformed our expectations, we currently expect 2026 ad revenue of ~$2.7 billion [versus] approximately $3 billion previously (due to slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities)," Netflix said.
(Scott Kanowsky contributed reporting)

title: Meta sued in Australian class action over alleged social media harm to children
full_text:

The lawsuit, filed in the Federal Court, Australia’s second-highest, by law firm MinterEllison this month could be the first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers.

• In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information which could reveal the identity of the applicants, and the statement of claim.
• The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
• Meta in August agreed to pay $18 billion to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims it designed social media to addict children.

title: Meta’s revenue beat; Tesla’s lower annual sales goal - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices slip, as traders pore through earnings from Facebook-owner Meta Platforms and Elon Musk-led electric car giant Tesla. Meta shares advance in extended-hours trading after the tech behemoth unveils better-than-expected quarterly revenue and robust current-quarter guidance. Shares of Tesla fall on a lower annual sales target, while some insiders reportedly express concerns over regulatory scrutiny of a possible merger between Tesla and Musk’s rocket firm SpaceX.
1. Futures dip
U.S. stock futures pointed lower on Thursday. By 03:08 ET (07:08 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had fallen by 75 points, or 1.0%, Nasdaq 100 futures had dropped by 510 points, or 1.7%, and Dow futures had retreated by 283 points, or 0.5%.
The main averages on Wall Street advanced in the prior session, buoyed by strong results from Musk’s rocket company SpaceX and server maker Super Micro Computer. The returns helped to assuage some recent concerns around the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade, although analysts at Deutsche Bank flagged that the decline in Nasdaq futures could be a sign that not all investors were reassured.
Jitters have surrounded the AI sector for several days, triggered by a combination of heavy debt-fueled spending on AI infrastructure and elevated borrowing costs. Roller-coaster movements in AI-exposed stocks have mirrored shifting sentiment around AI, especially after fresh corporate returns appear to indicate that demand for the nascent technology remains solid.
2. Meta rises after revenue beat
Shares of Meta crept higher in extended-hours trading after the Instagram-owner unveiled higher-than-anticipated third-quarter revenue and announced plans to create a new class of nonvoting stock to raise capital for its AI ambitions.
Along with resilience in its core advertising business, the well-received debut of Meta’s Muse AI assistant in September has helped bolster returns during a time when the tech titan is investing hundreds of billions of dollars into the AI race. Hopes have been high that Muse will eventually add $28.5 billion of incremental revenue by 2030, according to Truist Securities projections cited by the Wall Street Journal.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in a post-earnings call that roughly a fourth of people who have set up Muse use it on "any given day," particularly for shopping. Zuckerberg added that Meta is aiming to create a "large-scale Muse network," even though the app has been blocked on some websites, such as Amazon.com.
For the current quarter, Meta guided for revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, with the top end of the range exceeding Wall Street estimates. The firm also narrowed its capital expenditures forecast to $135 billion to $145 billion. The low end of the outlook was previously $130 billion.
3. Tesla sets lower sales target amid SpaceX merger speculation
Shares of Tesla fell after-hours, weighed down by the Musk-led EV group setting a lower goal for per-year sales by the end of the decade to 5 million units, while investors eyed the potential for a blockbuster tie-up with SpaceX.
Previously, Musk had guided for annual sales of 20 million vehicles. A potential multibillion-dollar tax bill
According to Meta’s filing, Zuckerberg informed a special committee of independent directors that he was considering moving his primary residence outside California in response to Proposition 40, a proposed one-time wealth tax on billionaires scheduled for consideration by California voters in November.
The company warned that the measure could expose Zuckerberg to a multibillion-dollar tax liability based on his Meta holdings. Paying such a bill could require him to sell shares, potentially reducing his voting power.
Meta’s concern was not simply that its founder might face a substantial tax payment. The committee considered it critically important that Zuckerberg continue leading the company from its California headquarters, particularly as Meta intensifies its investment in artificial intelligence.
The resulting agreement includes an eight-year commitment for Zuckerberg to remain resident in California, or another jurisdiction where Meta maintains its headquarters, subject to the agreement’s conditions and an exception for material unforeseen circumstances.
In exchange, Zuckerberg gains access to liquidity through the new Class C shares without immediately surrendering his majority voting control.
How Zuckerberg can unlock his wealth
Meta plans to distribute one Class C share for every existing Class A or Class B share. The initial distribution is a stock dividend, not a cash payment.
Zuckerberg will be able to sell or transfer 20% of the Class C shares he receives without the special sale restrictions imposed on the remainder. Meta says that portion represents approximately 10% of his overall economic stake in the company.
The proceeds from those sales would go to Zuckerberg personally, not to Meta. He can use the money for any purpose, including paying a potential California wealth-tax bill.
The remaining 80% will generally be subject to restrictions linking the transfer of Class C shares to the sale or conversion of an equivalent number of voting shares. An additional 2.5% of his original Class C allocation is released from those restrictions for each qualifying quarter in which he continues serving in the required leadership role, allowing the restriction to expire over eight years of qualifying service.
The distinction is important: Zuckerberg can monetize some of his economic ownership while maintaining his voting control, but the agreement places conditions on how quickly he can dispose of the remaining shares.
The bigger prize: a new source of AI capital
For Meta, the more consequential feature may be what it can do with Class C stock in the years ahead.
The company explicitly says it expects to conduct Class C equity offerings from time to time in the future. It also identifies the new shares as a financing instrument for acquisitions, employee compensation and other corporate purposes.
Meta says it faces an unprecedented need for capital as artificial intelligence transforms the technology industry. Its investments extend beyond developing AI models to the computing infrastructure required to train and operate them.
Reuters reported that Meta’s long-term forecasts, as described in the filing, envisaged raising hundreds of billions of dollars over several years to finance its AI-related growth plan.
Class C could give Meta another way to fund that expansion: sell new shares to outside investors in exchange for cash, without adding ordinary voting rights to the shareholder base.
That is fundamentally different from Zuckerberg selling his own shares. A founder’s sale transfers ownership between investors and provides no money to the company. A primary equity offering by Meta raises new cash that the company can deploy into its business.
The new class could also serve as currency in stock-funded acquisitions and employee awards. That flexibility may become increasingly valuable as technology companies compete for scarce AI talent, computing resources and strategic assets.
Meta’s $825 billion in spending commitments
As of September 30, 2026, Meta agreed to approximately $355.73 billion in leases that have not yet started, covering data centers, energy infrastructure, and network facilities.
These leases will begin over the next decade and can last up to 30 years. While these costs are not yet recorded as lease liabilities on its balance sheet, they represent substantial future payments that Meta will need to make.
On top of this, Meta has $454.52 billion in other contractual commitments, mainly for cloud computing, servers, network equipment, energy, and Reality Labs products. Around $45.85 billion is due in 2026 and $121.41 billion in 2027.
Meta also has potential cloud capacity purchases of up to $14.72 billion over five years.
The key takeaway is that Meta is committing enormous sums to future growth today. These investments could strengthen its position in AI and other technologies, but they also lock in significant future spending and leave Meta with less flexibility if business conditions change or the investments fail to deliver the expected returns.
The price of preserving control
The structure offers a clear governance advantage for Zuckerberg, but it does not eliminate the economic cost of raising equity capital.
Class C holders will generally have the same economic rights as Class A and Class B holders, but no ordinary voting rights. Because investors may value voting shares more highly, Class C could trade at a discount to Class A.
If that discount is substantial, Meta might need to issue more shares to raise the same amount of money, increasing economic dilution for existing shareholders.
The initial one-for-one dividend does not itself raise capital or change shareholders’ relative economic ownership. The dilution question arises when Meta subsequently sells newly issued Class C shares or uses them for acquisitions and employee compensation.
Meta also intends to establish a liquid trading market for Class C, partly to minimise any valuation discount. Whether that succeeds will depend on investor demand, trading liquidity and the market’s assessment of the rights attached to the shares.
A founder deal with lasting consequences
The arrangement illustrates how Meta is attempting to solve two problems simultaneously. Zuckerberg gets a means to access some of his wealth and an agreement that supports his continued residence near the company’s headquarters. Meta gets an additional financing instrument for what could become one of the most capital-intensive periods in its history.
The company’s independent directors have argued that retaining Zuckerberg’s leadership is particularly important as competition in AI accelerates. Yet the structure also prolongs the separation between economic ownership and voting control: investors can supply additional capital without gaining the voting influence that would ordinarily accompany a comparable issuance of Class A shares.
For shareholders, that is the central trade-off. Meta gains flexibility to finance AI development, acquisitions and talent without further diluting voting power. In return, investors must accept the possibility of economic dilution and a price discount on the new stock, alongside the continued concentration of control in Zuckerberg’s hands.
The California tax issue may have triggered the negotiations, but Class C could become a much larger strategic tool. If Meta’s AI ambitions demand hundreds of billions in additional capital, a publicly traded non-voting share class gives the company a way to seek that funding while preserving the governance structure its founder wants to retain.
The question is no longer simply whether Zuckerberg can afford to stay in California. It is whether Meta can use this new financial architecture to fund its AI future without asking investors to surrender more voting power—and whether those investors will consider that bargain worthwhile.

title: Analysis-How a merged SpaceX-Tesla might navigate its China problem
full_text:
Meta’s new Class C stock to keep Zuckerberg in California, fund AI spending spree
Oct 22 (Reuters) - Elon Musk’s potential mega-merger of Tesla and SpaceX would likely face a China-shaped hurdle from regulators on both sides of the Pacific over concerns about national security and the sharing of data and technology.
The world’s richest person said on Tuesday his two companies had set up special committees to discuss a union, calling a merger a “good idea”. Turning it into reality, however, would mean navigating the thorny issue of Tesla’s heavy reliance on China for manufacturing versus SpaceX’s defence business.
Rocket company SpaceX is increasingly reliant on sensitive US government and defence contracts, which could subject any merger involving Tesla’s business in China to intense scrutiny on national security grounds.
Chinese regulators also require Tesla to keep confidential user data collected by its automated driving systems firmly in China, and any firewall would have to prevent the flow of information or technology in either direction.
Below are some ways that Musk and the companies could look to clear any barriers put up by Washington or Beijing.
COULD TESLA KEEP ITS CHINA BUSINESS?
One potential option would be for the merged company to create a firewall around Tesla’s Chinese operations to block access to sensitive data from SpaceX and other parts of the business. Such a move is not unheard of, said Daniel Kollar, head of automotive and mobility practice at consultancy Intralink Group.
Plenty of companies have been able to run major defence businesses outside of China while maintaining operations in the country, he said, citing Airbus and Honeywell.
SpaceX’s defence-related businesses include Starshield, which develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
A two-way firewall would also likely be the minimum requirement to ensure Tesla’s data from Chinese drivers stays in China, analysts said. Since 2021, Tesla has been complying with Beijing’s requirement to keep all driver data inside of China.
Tesla could continue to operate in China for years to come as a self-contained unit with its own research and development and strict agreements to keep all data inside China, said Michael Dunne, CEO of automotive advisory firm Dunne Insights, which closely follows China’s auto industry.
Keeping both Beijing and Washington happy about such a firewall, however, could be tricky, said Christopher Tang, a professor at UCLA’s Anderson School of Management who specializes in global supply chains. He said the Chinese government is likely to try to use any proposed merger to negotiate a range of items as a condition for approval.
"China will use it as leverage," Tang said. "They have the bargaining power right now."
Ioannis Kokkoris, professor of competition law and economics at Queen Mary University of London, identified two possible concessions that China could seek: access for Chinese companies to strategically significant technologies, and commitments to retain manufacturing capacity and investment in China.
Any demand to share sensitive SpaceX-related technology, however, would run directly into US security restrictions.
WHAT ABOUT DIVESTMENT?
Analysts have said there were likely three broad paths towards divestment: a spinoff in which Tesla retains a majority economic interest, a sale paired with long-term brand licensing agreements, or an outright sale, possibly to another automaker.
Any kind of divestment would come with plenty of complications, including the looming question of who would buy the asset. China’s automakers, which do not need any extra capacity, are unlikely to be interested, said Li Yanwei, an analyst at the China Automobile Dealers Association.
Many foreign automakers, on the other hand, are already strapped for cash, making them unlikely buyers as well. Kollar said Musk would be more likely to sell the China operation off for parts rather than hand control to anyone else.
But Kollar added that unless Musk wanted to signal a retreat from the auto business, he expected Tesla to find a way to retain its China operations under the existing ownership structure.
Tesla China and China’s State Administration of Market Regulation did not reply to requests for comment.
CHINA STILL NEEDED FOR CASH FLOW
A clean break from China could be difficult. Chinese suppliers are deeply integrated in Musk’s broader empire and Tesla’s Shanghai production accounted for more than 50% of its global output, according to Yale Zhang, managing director at Shanghai-based consultancy AutoForesight.
Some investors, though, say those considerations aren’t big enough to get in the way of a deal.
Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, a Tesla and SpaceX investor, said Tesla’s China manufacturing base is considerable, but the electric vehicle maker has already been making moves to expand US production, particularly for humanoid robots and the Cybercab driverless car, and many investors are more focused on Musk’s promises for where these are headed.
Mulberry also said he thinks Tesla would argue to US regulators that its China operations wouldn’t overlap with SpaceX, but if unsuccessful, he thinks Tesla could shut or scale back its China production.
"It’s short-term enough and small enough to be digestible," he said.
Tang, the UCLA professor, said that while Tesla’s future prospects may lie outside of China, its current EV business is heavily reliant on it. Much of the cash needed to finance its future bets comes from China EV production, he said.
"That is exactly why China will take advantage of this moment," Tang said. "Because you still need them."

title: Steep bill for AI buildout punishes Meta, other tech favorites
full_text:
Nasdaq falls nearly 3% on elevated AI financing worries; oil gains and bonds rally
By Lewis Krauskopf and Sudeshna Ghoshal
NEW YORK, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The tab for the next round of the AI buildout came due on Thursday.
Investors sold shares of Meta Platforms and a wealth of companies central to the AI trade, a day after Meta — one of the hyperscalers spending billions to build data centers and other infrastructure supporting the AI boom — said it would issue a new class of shares that will help it raise funds.
Meta fell 8%, its largest drop since July. SpaceX declined 9% and semiconductor company Nvidia — a bellwether of the AI trade — dropped 4%. The Nasdaq Composite was on track for its largest decline in four months.
A 12% plunge in shares of semiconductor company Lam Research following its results also weighed on sentiment and sent the semiconductor index down 6.5%.
The pullback is the latest test for the AI trade, focusing on the rising costs of a long-term project the payoffs from which remain uncertain and will likely be unevenly distributed. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, but Wall Street now expects that higher interest rates mean the likes of Meta will sell billions of dollars in stock to fund the next round of building — putting pressure on share prices by increasing the number of shares outstanding.
It is an unwelcome development in a market where major US stock indexes remain near all-time highs despite a punishing month of volatile trading.
RETURN ON INVESTMENT CONCERNS
Selling started with "the big question about the (return on investment) on all the spending," said Matthew Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak. "It’s just becoming more and more evident to people that it’s going to take a lot longer."
Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital LLC in New York, agreed that ROI concerns are central while also citing remarks by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about a financing bottleneck for smaller AI companies as contributing to the selling.
Meta said on Wednesday it would use new Class C shares, which hold no voting power, to fund AI spending and other priorities. Meta also raised the low end of its annual spending forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion, with the high end unchanged at $145 billion.
That level of spending will require lots of investor participation in coming stock sales. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. It was the first cash burn at Meta in more than a decade.
“More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend (is) concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut.
The action highlights concern over how AI investment will be paid for. Credit default swaps tracking perceived default risk of many of the biggest AI players have risen over the past year, with Meta’s hitting a record on Thursday — reflecting uncertainty over who will benefit most from the sums being spent now.
Fresh signs of market pressure to curb spending on AI quickly translated on Thursday into a broad market selloff reflecting expectations that any AI pullback would hit US growth, resulting in a sharp rally in Treasury prices.
"This is your classic rotation day,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner, co-founder and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. “You can see the money going into Treasuries, so it’s a classic safety move ... They are rotating out of techs, out of the AIs, and into the more safety trades, whether it’s bonds or some of those big Dow Jones stocks.”
“To me, it’s people getting nervous, saying, OK I’m going to lighten up a little or rotate out for a while," Saluzzi added.
Thursday’s selloff added to the pressure on the neocloud companies at the heart of the AI buildout, with Nebius off 8% after announcing a new $3.5 billion credit line from Citigroup and CoreWeave, whose unsecured bond yields soared to 15% in last week’s AI selloff, down 11%.
Bank of America analyst Tal Liani said in a report on Thursday he maintains a buy rating and a price target of $140 on CoreWeave stock heading into next month’s earnings report, though he said he believes the firm will need to raise $20 billion to fund commitments to customers — the sort of prospect that is generating investor anxiety now across the technology industry.
"Nobody is worried about Meta or Amazon or Google getting the financing they need," Maley said. "But if it gets prohibitive for smaller companies, then you don’t have to have an implosion of things to make people nervous."

title: UK consumer confidence tumbles ahead of Healey’s budget, GfK reports
full_text:
Nasdaq posts worst day since June as AI financing worries batter risk sentiment
By Andy Bruce
Oct 23 (Reuters) - British consumer confidence has suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since early in the COVID-19 pandemic as economic worries deepen, according to a survey that created an unwelcome backdrop for finance minister John Healey’s budget next week.
GfK’s consumer confidence index dropped 11 points to -24 in October, its lowest since April and below all the forecasts from economists a Reuters poll. September’s reading of -13 was the highest since August 2024.
The drop was biggest from one month to the next since April 2020, just after Britain entered its first coronavirus lockdown. Excluding the pandemic, the last drop on this scale followed the June 2016 Brexit vote.
GfK said no single factor explained the slump and pointed instead to rising inflation, the conflict in the Middle East and the broader squeeze on household budgets.
Healey has said he wants to give households and businesses "breathing space" in his budget. He has struck an upbeat tone on the economy, pointing to growth in the first half of the year that was jointly the fastest in the Group of Seven.
But surveys this month from S&P Global and LSEG/Ipsos have also shown weaker consumer sentiment, undoing a recovery that took hold around the time Andy Burnham became prime minister.
"The speed of this deterioration is alarming," said Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK.
Households’ views of the wider economy and their appetite for big-ticket purchases deteriorated sharply with the major purchase index falling to its lowest in more than two years.
Consumers’ inflation expectations rose to their highest since April when they reached an almost 3-1/2-year peak. That is likely to concern the Bank of England, which is expected to raise interest rates next month.
GfK’s survey of 2,003 adults was conducted October 1-14.

title: Analysis-Musk’s political baggage clouds prospects for SpaceX-Tesla deal
full_text:
Nasdaq posts worst day since June as AI financing worries batter risk sentiment
By Cassell Bryan-Low and Hyunjoo Jin
Oct 22 (Reuters) - A possible merger between Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX and carmaker Tesla may face bigger obstacles from politics than from regulation, drawing scrutiny in Beijing and potentially igniting a battle between US President Donald Trump and the Democrats.
Musk revived speculation about a tie-up this week, calling a combination "a good idea" and confirming that committees at both companies were reviewing a potential deal, a step toward what could become the largest merger in history and create a company worth about $3.5 trillion.
But a merger would also unite one of the US government’s most important aerospace and defense contractors with one of the most China-exposed major American manufacturers — a combination likely to raise questions about national security risks both in Washington and in Beijing.
Those concerns are unlikely to derail a deal, analysts said, but they would likely leave the combined company exposed to years of political wrangling and pressure from both sides of the Pacific.
Tesla’s China operations, they said, could become a source of leverage for Beijing in any future dispute with Washington, while a Democratic takeover of the US House of Representatives in next month’s midterm elections could subject the deal to congressional investigations and political maneuvering.
Democrats immediately raised concerns about the deal’s implications, signaling their intent to turn the merger into a political flashpoint ahead of the November 3 midterms.
“If Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that antitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize," said US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat who sits on both the Judiciary and Foreign Relations committees.
He added that he was prepared to conduct oversight of any deal: "When one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too."
Musk could seek to address concerns by limiting how closely the two companies are integrated.
The greater threat to the deal may come later, however, if a future administration takes a harder line on the relationship between Tesla and a company increasingly tied to US national security, analysts said.
"A merger agreement would involve pledges of limits to the connections between SpaceX and Tesla," said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
"I don’t think the Trump administration would enforce these limits. However, the next administration could certainly begin to scrutinize a merged entity. This may be the biggest risk to a deal - that it could get unwound in 2029."
EXPOSURE TO CHINA
For Beijing, a merger would effectively place Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing hub under the same corporate umbrella as SpaceX, a company that has become deeply embedded in US military and national security activities through its Pentagon work and through Starlink’s role in conflicts, including Ukraine.
"A formal merger would make it harder for Chinese authorities to treat Tesla as a purely commercial actor, raising risks for future factory expansions, data approvals, or market access," said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, a senior research fellow at the Brussels-based Bruegel think tank.
Tesla’s reliance on production from Shanghai already gives China considerable leverage over Musk’s business empire. A merger could extend that control to a broader corporate group encompassing strategically important assets such as satellite communications, launch services and military-related technologies.
GLOBAL REGULATORY HURDLES
The deal would also have to navigate a maze of reviews around the world as competition authorities assess its impact on industries ranging from automobiles and satellite communications to artificial intelligence and semiconductors.
Musk’s close relationship with Trump would likely dispel concerns about potential US regulatory roadblocks to a transaction, analysts said, while antitrust experts see limited competition concerns because the companies operate largely in separate markets.
Outside the United States, however, foreign regulators are likely to scrutinize whether a combined company would gain an unfair advantage by integrating technologies spanning automobiles, artificial intelligence and aerospace.
Antitrust experts said authorities in markets with powerful domestic auto industries, such as China and South Korea, could examine whether Tesla’s access to SpaceX technologies would give it an advantage that rivals cannot replicate, creating barriers for competitors and potentially undermining domestic manufacturers.
Regulators could respond by requiring the company to license key technologies to competitors as part of any approval, said Ioannis Kokkoris, a law professor at Queen Mary University of London.
A South Korean antitrust official told Reuters that the merger, if pursued, could require an in-depth review of its potential impact on that country’s industries.
"Korean antitrust officials will be wary of the merger. They will take the merger very seriously," said Lee Hwang, a law professor at Korea University and former Korea Fair Trade Commission official.
"The stakes are very high in Korea because it regards both the automotive and aerospace sectors as strategically important industries."

title: SK Hynix says Solidigm drops plan for US IPO amid market volatility
full_text:
SEOUL, Oct 23 (Reuters) - South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix said on Friday that it decided against a US initial public offering for its Solidigm subsidiary, citing financial market volatility and recent share price trends.
SK Hynix said in a statement it would continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm’s expansion and enhance shareholder value, including reviewing the timing, scale and financing of future investments.
"This decision does not reflect any change in Solidigm’s growth prospects or investment needs," the company said.
Despite strong business performance at both SK Hynix and Solidigm, the company said increased market volatility and a broader correction in semiconductor stocks had prompted it to reconsider the listing.
The decision comes just weeks after SK Hynix said it was reviewing various options to strengthen Solidigm’s competitiveness, but that no decisions had been made.
Solidigm, based in Rancho Cordova, California, is SK Hynix’s US subsidiary specialising in NAND flash memory and solid-state drives.
SK Hynix had considered an IPO as one of several ways to finance Solidigm’s expansion amid growing demand for memory chips driven by artificial intelligence.
The company said raising external capital through a listing could have boosted its consolidated cash flow, helping fund new production facilities while supporting shareholder returns through dividends, share buybacks and share cancellations.
In addition, SK Hynix said an IPO could have helped investors better recognise Solidigm’s growth potential, which it said was not fully reflected in the parent company’s valuation.
